OpenAI shipped "dots," its new agentic avatar, the same day Meta said it's rolling Muse out to small businesses.

Two different labs, two different names, the same idea underneath: an assistant that logs into your accounts and keeps working after you shut your laptop.

That's not a feature update. That's a new category of software asking for your passwords. Before you touch either one, check what it can actually reach — and what happens if it reaches too far.

slides.text: Two AI agents launched the same day. Same idea.
An assistant that works after you close the laptop sounds helpful. The risk is what it's allowed to touch.
OpenAI's dots and Meta's Muse both sign into your tools, not just chat with you.
"Signing in" means it can open your email, your calendar, maybe your ad account. Which ones, you choose — if you check.
Every connected app has a permissions screen. Most people click allow without reading what it says.
That screen usually lists exactly what the agent can see and do — send messages, read files, post on your behalf.
An agent running your Meta ads unsupervised can spend your budget while you're asleep. Nobody told it your weekly limit.
None of this needs buying anything this month. It needs one habit before you connect a single agent to a business account.
Before you link any agent: open its permissions list, read every line, and remove any access it doesn't need for the one job you want it to do.
The news isn't that AI agents exist now. It's that two of the biggest labs shipped one on the same day, which means your clients will start asking about this before you've tested it.
Check permissions before you check promises. That's the whole method.
